meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Thank You for the Gift Book. I Shall Lose No Time In Reading It'?
meta.ogDescription: A Victorian joke with no owner: in print by 1871 from an unnamed botanist, pinned on Disraeli only in 1898 — 17 years after his death.

answer.label: Not Benjamin Disraeli — an anonymous Victorian joke
answer.authorDates: In print by 1871 · first credited to Disraeli in 1898
answer.sourceLine: This double-edged thank-you is a 19th-century joke that circulated for decades with no fixed author. The earliest humorous use found by Quote Investigator ↗ appeared in The British Quarterly Review in October 1871, where the wit is identified only as “a celebrated botanist.” Disraeli’s name was attached in 1898, and even his sympathetic 1903 biographer, Wilfrid Meynell, printed the line while admitting there was little evidence of its “paternity” ↗.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from

docMeta.dd: “A Scotchman”, in Max O’Rell’s Friend Mac Donald, 1887

source.excerpt: A celebrated botanist used to return thanks somewhat in the following form:—‘I have received your book, and shall lose no time in reading it.’ The unfortunate author might put his own construction on this rather ambiguous language.
trail: The earliest humorous use Quote Investigator ↗ locates is an October 1871 item in The British Quarterly Review, which credits only “a celebrated botanist” — no name is given.

The oldest telling we could read in full is Max O’Rell’s Friend Mac Donald (Bristol, 1887), page 32, which gives it to an unnamed Scotchman: “Many thanks for the book which you did me the honour to send me. I will lose no time in reading it.” Read the scan at the Internet Archive ↗.

Disraeli’s name enters in 1898, in a New York Times books column reporting that Lord Beaconsfield had “a kind of stereotyped form of acknowledgment, somewhat ambiguous in phraseology,” per Quote Investigator ↗.

Wilfrid Meynell’s Benjamin Disraeli: An Unconventional Biography (1903) prints “Many thanks: I shall lose no time in reading it” and then hedges: “This ambiguity, fathered upon Disraeli, might very well be his; and if there is as little evidence of the paternity as that which sometimes satisfies a magistrate of sentiment, we can say ‘Ben trovato’ in all truth.” Read the page at the Internet Archive ↗.
source.excerptNote: The earliest humorous instance located by Quote Investigator ↗, in The British Quarterly Review (October 1871), where the wit is left unnamed. None of the documented 19th-century tellings uses the modern “thank you for the gift book” wording.

source.rightsNote: No single authored source underlies this line. It circulated anonymously from at least 1871, and the modern “gift book” wording matches none of the documented 19th-century texts, so no copyright status can be asserted for it. The printed sources that carry the older forms — The British Quarterly Review (1871), Friend Mac Donald (1887) and Meynell’s biography (1903) — are themselves long in the public domain.

author.name: Anonymous
author.heading: About the author — and why there isn’t one
author.metaLine: Unidentified · earliest humorous use in The British Quarterly Review, October 1871
author.bio: Nobody knows who first turned this thank-you into a weapon. It surfaces in 1871 as the habit of an unnamed “celebrated botanist” and spends the next sixty years being reassigned — to a Scotchman, a bishop, two Prime Ministers, and a string of literary men — without any of them leaving a letter that contains it. Quote Investigator’s judgement is that the phrase was rarely used in a real reply at all, and lived mainly in comic anecdote.

copyAttribution: An anonymous Victorian joke, in print by 1871 — often misattributed to Benjamin Disraeli, who was first credited with it in 1898.

misattribution.heading: Why Disraeli gets the credit — and why it does not hold
misattribution.intro: Disraeli was a novelist as well as a Prime Minister, and was genuinely deluged with unsolicited manuscripts, which makes the story feel right. But the joke was already in print, unattached to him, for nearly thirty years before his name was fixed to it.

items.why: No letter, diary or contemporary account in Disraeli’s hand contains the line. The first ascription to him is a New York Times column of 1898, seventeen years after his death in 1881, and it reports only a “stereotyped form of acknowledgment” at second hand, per Quote Investigator ↗.

The British Quarterly Review printed the quip in October 1871 with no name attached, and Quote Investigator ↗ has found no earlier humorous use — and no direct evidence, in the form of a letter from any prominent person, that anyone actually sent it.

items.who: Wilberforce, Gladstone, Aldrich, Holmes, Thackeray, Hadas
items.why: The same joke was pinned on Bishop Samuel Wilberforce (1894), William Gladstone (1897), Thomas Bailey Aldrich (1900), Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr. (1902), W. M. Thackeray (1931) and the classicist Moses Hadas (1982). A quip that attaches to eight famous names across more than a century belongs to none of them, per Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: It is an anonymous Victorian joke, in print by 1871 and never traced to any letter Disraeli actually wrote, per Quote Investigator ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line survives because it solves a real problem with perfect deniability: how to acknowledge a book you have no intention of reading, in words the sender cannot object to. “I shall lose no time in reading it” can mean I will start at once or I will never begin, and the sentence itself refuses to say which.

That is also why it never stayed with one teller. Victorian magazines traded it as a stock item — Punch listed it in 1890 among phrases printed with their real meanings, glossing it “No; not a single second” — and each retelling simply attached whichever famous wit the reader would find plausible.
detailsBody: The phrase was not always a joke. Quote Investigator ↗ notes a 1784 letter by the poet William Cowper using “lose no time in reading it” entirely straightforwardly. The comic version depends on the reader noticing the ambiguity, which is why the earliest tellings bother to explain it: the 1871 text adds that “the unfortunate author might put his own construction on this rather ambiguous language.”
context.pull: A joke that fits eight famous names across more than a century belongs to none of them.

Meynell's 1903 biography prints 'Many thanks: I shall lose no time in reading it' and concedes there is little evidence of 'the paternity'.
